content: The quality of evidence supporting the potential benefits of male circumcision for this population was rated as poor. Further high-quality studies are necessary to confirm any potential advantages. Unprotected sexual intercourse exposes women to risks of sexually transmitted diseases (STDs) and unintended pregnancies. Healthcare providers managing such cases should offer counseling on the option of emergency contraception (EC) if pregnancy is not desired. In the United States, EC options include the copper intrauterine device (IUD) and emergency contraceptive pills (ECPs). ECPs can be taken as a single dose or as two doses (each 75 mg, taken 12 hours apart), or as a combination of estrogen and progestin (Yuzpe regimen). Some ECPs are available over the counter, while others can be provided through advance prescriptions or directly by healthcare providers. Emergency insertion of a copper IUD within five days of unprotected intercourse can reduce the risk of pregnancy by more than 99%. ECPs are most effective when initiated as soon as possible after unprotected intercourse but retain some efficacy up to five days later. However, ECPs are ineffective (though not harmful) if the woman is already pregnant. A 2012 Cochrane review summarized the efficacy, safety, and convenience of various EC methods. Additional information on EC can be found in the 20th edition of Contraceptive Technology. Postexposure prophylaxis (PEP) guidelines for preventing HIV and other STDs following sexual exposure are discussed in another section of this report. Practices such as vaginal washing and douching after sexual exposure are ineffective in protecting against HIV and STDs and may increase the risk of bacterial vaginosis (BV), certain STDs, and HIV infection. The randomized controlled trial HPTN 052 demonstrated that in HIV-serodiscordant heterosexual couples, antiretroviral therapy (ART) in the HIV-infected partner reduces the risk of transmission to the uninfected partner by 96%. Therefore, ART not only benefits the health of individuals with HIV infection but also significantly reduces the risk of ongoing transmission. For these reasons, treatment should be offered to all individuals with HIV infection. The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services provides HIV treatment guidelines. Providing herpes simplex virus (HSV) treatment to individuals co-infected with HIV and HSV has not been shown to reduce HIV acquisition in uninfected partners. A large randomized controlled trial involving 3,408 serodiscordant heterosexual couples in Africa, where the HIV-infected partner was also HSV-2 seropositive, evaluated the use of acyclovir (400 mg twice daily) versus placebo. The primary outcome was HIV transmission to the uninfected partner. Acyclovir use had no effect on HIV transmission. These findings are consistent with a previous trial that found no benefit of acyclovir in preventing HIV-1 acquisition in HSV-2 seropositive individuals. Certain large, randomized, placebo-controlled trials have demonstrated the safety and substantial efficacy of daily oral antiretroviral preexposure prophylaxis (PrEP) using a fixed-dose combination of tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) and emtricitabine (FTC). These trials showed significant reductions in HIV acquisition rates among men who have sex with men (MSM), HIV-serodiscordant heterosexual couples, and heterosexual men and women recruited as individuals. Additional trials involving injection drug users (IDUs) and heterosexual HIV-serodiscordant couples demonstrated the efficacy and safety of daily oral PrEP with TDF alone when combined with repeated condom provision, sexual risk-reduction counseling, and the diagnosis and treatment of STDs. High adherence to oral PrEP with TDF alone or in combination with FTC was strongly associated with protection against HIV infection. Data suggest that when administered orally, TDF levels are lower in vaginal tissue compared to rectal tissue, potentially explaining why high adherence was necessary to achieve benefits among women in these trials.
